questions.q: Why does `pricing_core.hpp` deliberately avoid including any pybind11 header?
options: pybind11 headers are only valid inside a .cpp file, never a .hpp file
So the pricing core remains ordinary, independently buildable and testable C++ with no dependency on Python
Because header files cannot contain function definitions in C++
Because Black-Scholes formulas require C-style headers only
questions.explain: Keeping the pricing core free of pybind11 headers means it compiles and can be unit-tested as plain C++, with the Python integration layered on separately in bindings.cpp.

questions.q: In `MonteCarloEngine::priceCall`, why does each `std::async` task seed its own independent `std::mt19937_64` rather than sharing one random engine across threads?
options: Shared state like a single RNG instance being mutated from multiple threads concurrently is a data race; giving each task its own engine avoids needing any mutex
std::mt19937_64 cannot be constructed more than once in a program
Sharing one RNG would make the Monte Carlo result deterministic in a way that's undesirable
pybind11 forbids calling std::async more than once per module
questions.explain: A single RNG object mutated by multiple threads without synchronization is a classic data race. Giving each async task its own seeded engine avoids any shared mutable state, so no lock is required.

questions.q: What does calling `.get()` on each `std::future<double>` returned by `std::async` do?
options: It cancels the asynchronous task immediately
It blocks the calling thread until that task completes, then returns its result
It restarts the task from the beginning
It has no effect unless the task has already thrown an exception
questions.explain: `std::future::get()` blocks until the associated asynchronous task finishes and then returns (or rethrows, if the task threw) its result — this is how `priceCall` joins all the chunk results together.

questions.q: In the bindings layer, why does `py::class_<MonteCarloEngine>(m, "MonteCarloEngine").def("price_call", [](...) { ... })` use a lambda instead of binding `&MonteCarloEngine::priceCall` directly?
options: Lambdas run faster than member function pointers in every case
`priceCall` takes a `BlackScholesInputs` struct as one argument, and the lambda adapts separate keyword arguments (spot, strike, rate, vol, expiry) into that struct before calling it
pybind11 cannot bind any const member function directly
MonteCarloEngine has no member function named priceCall
questions.explain: The lambda exists purely to translate the five separate Python-facing keyword arguments into the single `BlackScholesInputs` struct that the underlying C++ method actually expects.

questions.q: What does `find_package(Threads REQUIRED)` combined with `target_link_libraries(quantpricer_cpp PRIVATE Threads::Threads)` accomplish in the CMakeLists.txt?
options: It installs Python's threading module
It locates and links the platform's native threading library so code using `std::async` and `std::thread` links and runs correctly
It disables multithreading to avoid data races
It is unnecessary boilerplate with no functional effect
questions.explain: `std::thread`/`std::async` require linking against the platform threading library (e.g. pthreads on Linux); `find_package(Threads REQUIRED)` locates it and `target_link_libraries` links it into the extension.
